children.text: The assessment, preparation and installation are described in writing before the work is agreed.

We check the existing material, depth and coverage, including gaps, compression and areas disturbed by earlier work. Accessible ceiling penetrations, eave ventilation and signs of moisture or roof leaks are considered together. Cold rooms, ice dams and earlier leaks help direct the assessment.

Preparation follows the written estimate: access and protection, any agreed removal, the listed air-sealing work and baffles at vented eaves. Related roof leakage or ventilation repairs are identified separately so fresh insulation does not cover an unresolved problem.

The selected product is installed to the agreed R-value, depth and coverage, with clear access retained for future service. The completion record identifies the material added and treated areas, and the work includes cleanup.

Plan Your Attic Insulation
Signs your attic is under-insulated
Uneven rooms, winter ice dams and high energy use can point to attic heat loss. One symptom can have several causes; the attic assessment looks at insulation, air leakage and moisture together.
Details for Your Attic Plan
Uneven rooms

Hot or cold ceilings, room-to-room temperature differences, drafts and dust are useful observations to bring to the visit. We compare those symptoms with insulation coverage and accessible air-leak pathways.
Ice dams in winter

Meltwater refreezes at the colder roof edge and can back up beneath the shingles. Air sealing, insulation and a clear ventilation path can help address contributing conditions. For ice or an active leak now, start with ice dam removal.
High heating or cooling bills
Results depend on the house, existing insulation, air leakage, equipment and heating and cooling use. The assessment identifies practical improvements without promising a fixed bill reduction.
What you can see in the attic

Visible clues include exposed joist tops, bare areas, insulation moved by earlier work, staining and roof-deck moisture. Observe only from a safe access point. Wet insulation, deteriorated framing, suspected contamination or old knob-and-tube wiring need assessment before new material covers them.
Guidance and Program Resources
ENERGY STAR Attic Air Sealing
Recommended R-values for Columbus

R-value measures resistance to heat flow. ENERGY STAR’s retrofit guidance gives the same attic additions for zones 4A/4B and 5, covering the climate-zone classifications used for Franklin County. These are retrofit recommendations, separate from a project’s applicable code requirements.
Attic with little or no insulation

The recommended addition provides a starting point for an empty attic floor. The product, installed depth and coverage must work together to deliver the planned performance; the estimate records the material and design target.
Attic with 3–4 inches already in place

This is an added-insulation recommendation, not a finished-total target of R-49. The existing material is evaluated for condition and insulating value before the proposed addition and completed installation target are recorded.
Depth isn't the same as R-value
Gaps, compression and uneven coverage affect performance. The written estimate names the product, treated areas, installed coverage and R-value rather than relying on an inch measurement alone.
ENERGY STAR Recommended Insulation Additions
Air sealing comes first

Insulation slows heat flow through the ceiling; air sealing addresses the gaps that let indoor air escape. EPA recommends air sealing before adding attic insulation, while the ceiling connections remain accessible.
Where attic air leaks hide

Common locations include plumbing and wire penetrations, recessed lights, flue and duct chases, kneewalls, dropped soffits and the attic hatch. The proposed work identifies the accessible leakage points to be addressed.
Sealing around heat sources

Air sealing around hot flues requires the correct noncombustible details and high-temperature sealant. Recessed lights must have the appropriate rating before insulation contacts them. These conditions are evaluated before insulation is added.
How it shows up in your estimate
Locations, materials and responsibility are recorded alongside insulation and baffle work. That makes the included preparation clear before a deeper layer covers the ceiling plane.
Insulation types: what we install and the alternatives

Roof King installs blown-in insulation and batts or rolls. We compare access, joist layout, obstructions and existing material to choose the appropriate installation. Other insulation systems have different applications and preparation requirements.
Insulation Options and Applications
Blown-in (loose-fill) insulation

It suits open attic floors, topping up a suitable existing layer and areas with wiring or other obstructions. Vented eaves need baffles and containment so material stays out of the soffit air path. The estimate identifies the selected product and installed performance.
Batts and rolls

Straightforward joist spacing can suit batts or rolls. Gaps and compression reduce their performance. Additional layers are planned with the existing material and facing, including unfaced batts where installed over suitable loose fill.
Other materials you may see in quotes

Spray foam can insulate and seal particular cavities or roofline assemblies. Rigid foam panels are used in specified building-envelope assemblies. Reflective barriers reduce radiant heat gain and are most useful in hot, sunny conditions. Compare the assembly, moisture control and application when weighing these alternatives.
ENERGY STAR Attic Insulation Guidance
Ventilation, baffles and your roof

A vented attic needs an open airflow path alongside the insulation. Air entering at the eaves and leaving through the designed exhaust helps manage heat and moisture; adding material must not block that route.
Keep the soffit vents open
Air must be able to move from the soffit into the intended channel under the roof deck. Keeping that route clear is part of preparing vented eaves for an insulation upgrade.
Baffles (rafter vents)

Baffles separate the insulation from the eave ventilation path. With blown-in material, containment at the top plate may also be needed to keep insulation out of the soffit. The estimate identifies new baffles and related preparation.
When the roof side needs work

Moist air should not discharge into the attic. Roof-side leakage or ventilation repairs are listed separately, and adding vents is not assumed to solve every moisture problem. Explore roof repair and roof replacement for the related roofing work.
ENERGY STAR Attic Ventilation
Removal, permits and incentives

Existing-material condition, the full construction work and program eligibility affect the plan. Address removal and approvals before installation, and check assistance eligibility before committing to a program-funded project.
Removing old or damaged insulation

The assessment explains what stays, what comes out and why. Roof leaks and persistent dampness need attention first. Suspected hazardous material or contamination requires the appropriate assessment and specialist handling before the insulation work proceeds.
Permits in Columbus

Columbus lists roof replacement as a permit project and finishing an attic as requiring a permit and plan review. An insulation-only upgrade differs from converting the attic to living space. Confirm the full project’s requirements with Columbus Building and Zoning Services before construction; surrounding municipalities use their own departments.
Tax credits and utility programs in 2026

The federal Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit applies to eligible improvements made through 2025 and is not offered here for a 2026 installation. Columbia Gas of Ohio’s WarmChoice program can include insulation and air sealing for income-qualified customers, subject to its assessment and eligibility rules. AEP Ohio also publishes household assistance programs. Applications and approved providers follow the utility’s requirements; Roof King does not determine eligibility or promise a rebate.

What Happens During an Attic Insulation Visit
The assessment, preparation and installation are described in writing before the work is agreed.
Assessing the Existing Attic

We check the existing material, depth and coverage, including gaps, compression and areas disturbed by earlier work. Accessible ceiling penetrations, eave ventilation and signs of moisture or roof leaks are considered together. Cold rooms, ice dams and earlier leaks help direct the assessment.
Preparing Before New Insulation

Preparation follows the written estimate: access and protection, any agreed removal, the listed air-sealing work and baffles at vented eaves. Related roof leakage or ventilation repairs are identified separately so fresh insulation does not cover an unresolved problem.
Installing to the Planned Performance

The selected product is installed to the agreed R-value, depth and coverage, with clear access retained for future service. The completion record identifies the material added and treated areas, and the work includes cleanup.
What Your Attic Insulation Estimate Includes
A useful estimate records the attic findings and proposed work so you can compare equivalent installations.
Assessment findings, access route and protection
Named insulation material, treated areas and planned R-value addition
Installed depth, coverage and completed installation target

Comparing Two Estimates

Compare the insulation product and planned performance alongside air sealing, baffles, removal and access. An insulation-only price does not describe the same work as a proposal that also prepares the ceiling plane and protects the ventilation path.
Repairs Found in the Attic
A roof leak, damaged material or a ventilation problem is documented and priced separately. Related roof repair is approved before the insulation installation covers the affected area.
Can insulation be added over existing material?

Often, yes, when the existing layer is dry, undamaged and suitable, and any leak or moisture problem has been addressed. The installation plan explains what remains, what needs removal and how the new material fits the existing layer.
How much attic insulation does a Columbus home need?

ENERGY STAR recommends adding R-60 in an uninsulated attic and adding R-49 where 3–4 inches already exist for the relevant climate zones. The R-49 figure is an addition, not the finished total. We assess the existing material and record the proposed addition and completed installation target.
Should air sealing be done before adding insulation?
Yes. EPA recommends air sealing first, while gaps at the ceiling plane are accessible. The estimate identifies the air-sealing locations and preparation included with the insulation work.
What types of insulation does Roof King install?
Roof King installs blown-in insulation and batts or rolls. Access, joist spacing, obstructions, the existing layer and the intended coverage help determine which installation fits your attic.
Will new insulation stop ice dams?

Insulation can help address heat loss, but recurring ice dams can also involve air leakage, ventilation, roof conditions and weather. Air sealing and insulation are considered together. For ice or a leak at the roof edge now, explore ice dam removal.
Do I need a permit for attic insulation in Columbus?

Requirements depend on the complete project and the property’s jurisdiction. Columbus requires a permit for roof replacement and permit plus plan review for finishing an attic. An insulation upgrade is different from a living-space conversion; project requirements are established before work begins.
Is there a tax credit or rebate for attic insulation in 2026?

The federal Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit covered eligible work through 2025 and is not included as an incentive for a 2026 installation. Columbia Gas of Ohio’s WarmChoice program may include insulation and air sealing for income-qualified customers. Utility programs determine eligibility, approved work and providers; review their current terms before relying on assistance.
Will the work lower my energy bills by a set amount?

Savings depend on the house, existing insulation and air leakage, heating and cooling equipment and household use. The estimate identifies the work and installed performance rather than promising a fixed reduction in bills.

Columbus requires attached decks to resist both vertical and horizontal movement. The attachment can't rely on toenails or nails that can pull out. Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

Usually, yes. The City of Columbus requires a permit and plan review for a new deck. The only exception is a deck that is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade, not attached to the house and not serving the required exit door. Decks over 169 square feet also need zoning approval. Suburbs set their own rules.
Does my deck need a railing?

In Columbus, a deck more than 30 inches above grade (measured 3 feet out from the edge) needs a 36- inch guard. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.
Is composite decking hotter than wood?

Composite gets hot in direct sun, and darker colors run hotter. Trex's heat-mitigating boards, such as Transcend Lineage and certain Select and Enhance colors, stay cooler than its original boards but can still get hot on summer afternoons.
Can I stain or paint a Trex deck?

Current Trex decking is designed for cleaning rather than periodic staining. Painting or staining can affect fade-and-stain coverage, and sanding can damage the surface. Identify the product line and follow its specific care instructions; older composite lines have different cleaning limits.
Can I put a fire pit on a composite deck?
Not a wood-burning one sitting directly on the boards. Trex notes its decking can soften at temperatures as low as 176°F. Check the product's instructions before placing any heat source on the deck.
Which warranty covers my deck?

Manufacturer product coverage and Roof King’s five-year workmanship coverage are separate. Trex residential decking terms vary by line, generally from 25 to 50 years. Your written estimate identifies the selected line and applicable coverage; keep both warranty documents with the project records.
Do you work on decks outside Columbus?
Yes, we serve communities across central Ohio. See our service areas. Permit rules change at city limits, so your estimate should say which building department applies.
How do I get a deck estimate?
Call (614) 490-0123 or book a time online. Estimates are free. Tell us whether you're planning a new deck or have an existing one to repair, resurface or refinish.

Choosing A Railing
Six questions narrow the choice for most decks. Bring your answers to the inspection.
Planning and Installation Details
The View

Cable (Signature X-Series) and frameless glass give the clearest view at seated eye level. Framed glass and Rod Rail are close behind. Rods and cables read as horizontal lines. Balusters and mesh give more privacy and a more traditional look. Glass panels need regular cleaning to stay clear.
Maintenance

Aluminum, steel, composite, glass and cable infill each call for different surface care. Check for loose caps, damaged connectors and post movement after storms or heavy use, and keep the exact railing model on record so replacement parts and cleaning methods match. A painted or stained wood railing also needs refinishing as its coating wears. Our deck refinishing page covers wood upkeep. If you keep a wood deck, a Trex railing can still go on it. See tab 4.
Budget

Line and infill: Trex describes Enhance as budget-friendly and Select T-Rail as near vinyl in cost. Signature glass and cable sit at the other end. Linear feet of railing, plus the count of corners, gates and stair sections. Posts and blocking: every guard post needs a solid attachment to the framing. Lighting added to posts and stairs, and any repairs found at the inspection.
Code

City of Columbus BZS memo CIC #23 quotes Residential Code of Ohio 312.1. It requires "a 36 inch high guardrail" on decks where the grade is more than 30 inches below the deck surface, measured 3 feet out from the edge. The American Wood Council's deck guide adds that openings must not let a 4-inch sphere pass, including under built-in benches. It also recommends measuring guard height from a fixed seat rather than the deck surface. Trex Select comes in 36- and 42- inch heights.
Stairs

Handrail 34 to 38 inches high, on at least one side, when there are 4 or more risers (RCO 311.7.7). Risers no more than 8¼ inches. Treads at least 9 inches deep. Open risers must not pass a 4-inch sphere (RCO 311.7.4). The AWC guide calls for a graspable handrail that runs continuously over the full flight.
Matching The House

Rail and post colors vary by line, and boards that have weathered won't match a new sample exactly. Compare real samples outside, next to your siding and trim. The deck visualizer helps you try combinations before the inspection.
Lighting, Fasteners, Fascia And Drainage
These four Trex accessories are planned before the boards go down. Wiring, clips, trim and drainage are much harder to add once the deck is closed in.
Deck And Stair Lighting

Trex says its lights run on 24 volts rather than 120-volt household current, use LEDs, and plug into a standard outlet through a transformer. A photocell timer runs the lights dusk to dawn or for 2, 4 or up to 10 hours, and a remote dimmer is available. Trex lists a 5-year limited warranty on its lights and transformers. Accent lights don't replace the stair light the code expects. The AWC guide (citing IRC R303.7) calls for a light source at the top landing that lights all the stairs, switched from inside the house. Motion or timer switches are acceptable.
Hidden Or Face Fastening

Trex's Universal Hidden Fastener is self-gapping and comes with a stainless steel screw already installed. Clips only work on boards with grooved edges. Stair treads, picture-frame borders and fascia use color-matched composite screws and plugs instead. The estimate names which fastener goes where.
Fascia And Finished Edges

Trex makes fascia in 1×8 and 1×12 boards, 12 feet long, and says it offers matching fascia for every Trex decking color plus Universal White. It needs no sanding, staining or painting. It's a trim board fastened over the rim, so the rim behind it still has to be sound.
Under-Deck Drainage

Trex says RainEscape keeps rain, spills and snowmelt from dripping through the boards and lets you create a dry patio or storage area below. It comes in brown or black, and Trex lists a 25-year warranty. It sits below the boards, so routing is settled before the walking surface goes down. On an existing deck, ask whether boards need to come up.

Adding To An Existing Deck
Many Columbus projects keep the deck and replace the railing, add stair lights or close in the underside. Whether that works depends on what's holding the railing, not on the boards you can see.
New Railing On A Wood Deck

Trex Select post sleeves slide over a 4×4 pressure-treated post. Trex says Select railings go over the deck frame or on the inside of the rim joist. Notched posts and posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist are not allowed. Blocking must be added for extra strength. Aluminum lines use their own post mounts, so we check the framing under each post before ordering.
Posts And The Rim

The American Wood Council's deck guide calls for guard posts of at least 4×4 attached to joists or rim joists of at least 2×8, with hold-down anchors rated for at least 1,800 pounds for a 36-inch guard. It notes that the IRC requires guards to resist a 200-pound load in any direction. Soft or split rim boards are repaired before a new railing goes on. That work is priced on its own line. See deck repair.
Ledger And House Connection

CIC #23 quotes RCO 502.2.2: attached decks must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and the attachment can't rely on toenails or nails subject to withdrawal. It also quotes RCO 703.8, which requires corrosion-resistant flashing where a deck meets a wood-frame wall. If the ledger or flashing is failing, fixing it comes before new railing.
Moving Or Adding Stairs

Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to the exit route between the door and the yard, including decks, landings and stairs. Landings and stairs 30 inches or less above grade can be issued a simpler minor permit that needs a final inspection when the work is done. Plan the new stair position around doors, furniture and the path into the yard.

How high does a deck railing have to be in Columbus?

At least 36 inches, when the deck surface is more than 30 inches above the ground measured 3 feet out from the edge. That's Residential Code of Ohio 312.1, as quoted in the City of Columbus deck memo (CIC #23). Stair handrails are 34 to 38 inches high when there are four or more risers.
Do I need a permit to replace my deck railing?

Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to decks, landings and stairs that form the exit route from a door, and a permit with plan review to build a deck. Whether a same-for-same railing swap needs one depends on the work, so call Columbus Building and Zoning Services or ask us to check before work starts.
Can I put a Trex railing on my wood deck?

Usually, yes. Trex Select post sleeves fit over 4×4 pressure-treated posts. Trex requires added blocking and doesn't allow notched posts or posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist. We check the posts and rim first, and any repairs are listed separately.
Which railing gives the best view?
Cable (Signature X-Series) and frameless glass keep the view most open, with framed glass and Rod Rail close behind. Glass needs cleaning to stay clear. Balusters and mesh give more privacy.
What's the difference between Trex Signature, Transcend, Select and Enhance?

Signature is aluminum with baluster, glass, mesh, rod and cable options. Transcend is a substantial composite rail. Select offers composite and metal options, and Enhance is Trex's value line in composite or steel. Trex lists warranties of 50 years for Signature, 35 for Transcend, 25 for most Select and for Enhance composite, and 15 for Enhance steel.
Can I add lighting to an existing deck?

Often, yes. Trex says post cap and stair riser lights can be added to an existing deck, while under-rail lights go in with the railing. The lights run on 24 volts through a plug-in transformer, so we plan the wire route and the outlet location.
Is under-deck drainage worth it?

It is if you want to use the space below an upper deck as a dry patio or for storage. Trex RainEscape catches water under the boards and carries it to downspouts. It goes in below the boards, so it's easiest during a new deck or a resurfacing.
Do hidden fasteners work on every board?
No. Hidden clips need boards with grooved edges. Square-edge boards, stair treads and fascia use color-matched screws and plugs. Your estimate states which fastener is used where.

expectedBlocks: A new deck has to work for the way you live and meet the requirements for your address. Roof King plans the door, furniture and stair layout alongside footings, framing and the house connection. Choose Trex, cedar or pressure-treated boards, then identify the construction and finishing details in a free written estimate.
How a New Deck Is Planned and Built
Six decisions shape a new deck. Explore the layout, supporting structure, boards and finishing details before the plans and material order are finalized.
Size And Layout
Size a deck from the activities it has to hold, then check the result against the City's thresholds. A few square feet can change which approvals you need.
Planning and Installation Details
Furniture First, Then The Footprint

Measure the furniture with chairs pulled out, not pushed in. Keep the door swing and the stair top clear of seating. Separate zones, such as dining and lounging, can be divided by a landing or a change in level.
Sizes That Change The Paperwork

The City requires zoning approval for any deck over 169 square feet, whatever its height or location. The only deck that skips the building permit and plan review is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade at any point, not attached to the house, and not serving the required exit door. Most attached decks need a permit at any size.
Height, Guards And The First Step

A 36-inch guard is required where the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge. The step down from the door threshold to the deck can be no more than 8¼ inches, provided the door doesn't swing out onto the deck.
Stairs And Where They Land

Risers can be no more than 8¼ inches and treads at least 9 inches. Open risers can't pass a 4-inch sphere. Four or more risers need a 34- to 38-inch handrail on at least one side. Stair stringers must bear on footings or a post-supported bearing block, not on a patio slab that isn't founded below frost depth.
Multiple Levels

prescriptive deck guide (DCA 6) covers single-level decks only. It notes that stairs between levels add loads its span tables don't consider. A multi-level design is planned and drawn for plan review rather than built from a standard table.
References for This Topic

Requirements apply to the property’s jurisdiction and the selected product. City of Columbus Deck and Egress Requirements · Ohio Residential Code: Floor and Deck Construction · Trex Installation and Care Resources
Attached Or Freestanding
How a deck connects to the house is the biggest structural decision you'll make. It sets the footings, the fasteners, the flashing and sometimes the permit path.
Ledger-Attached Deck

Works when the band joist is solid framing that bears fully on the foundation or wall below. Siding is removed at the ledger so it can be flashed. The attachment must resist vertical and horizontal movement; toenails or nails that can pull out are not allowed. The AWC prescriptive guide describes lateral hold-downs in at least two places within 2 feet of the deck edges, each rated at 1,500 pounds or more.
Non-Ledger Deck (Beam At The House)

The AWC prescriptive guide describes this approach where a ledger isn't allowed: brick, stone or masonry veneer, hollow masonry, or a cantilevered floor or bay window. Those posts sit close to the house. Footings within 5 feet of the foundation must bear at the same depth as the house footing. With a basement next to the deck, that means deep footings.
Fully Freestanding Deck

The building code says that if a positive connection to the house can't be verified at inspection, the deck must be self-supporting. A freestanding deck in Columbus can avoid the building permit only if it's 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval still applies above 169 square feet.
Which One Fits Your House

Vinyl, fiber-cement or wood siding over wood framing: a ledger is often possible once the band joist is confirmed. Brick or stone veneer, a bay window or a cantilevered floor: the code doesn't allow a ledger there, so use a non-ledger beam. A deck in the yard, away from the house: freestanding.
Footings And Framing
Footings, posts, beams and joists carry the deck. The design follows the local frost-depth requirements, soil conditions and the loads and support spacing for the selected materials.
Footings Below the Local Frost Depth

Footing design also considers the load, soil, nearby foundations and buried utilities. We identify utility locations before excavation and arrange the required footing inspection before the concrete is placed.
Footing Size

the deck area a post carries (its tributary area) and the soil's bearing capacity. Where weak soil is likely, the building official can require a soils investigation. A bigger deck or a longer beam span means bigger footings, not just more of them.
Posts And Beams

DCA 6 uses 6x6 posts as the minimum. The Ohio code ties maximum post height to post size and requires posts to be restrained at the footing with connectors or embedment. Beams need full bearing: at least 1½ inches on wood or metal and 3 inches on concrete.
Joist Spacing For The Boards You Choose
Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when boards run diagonally. The Ohio code ties wood-decking joist spacing to board thickness.
Lumber For Columbus Conditions

Ground-contact members, cut ends, flashing and connector compatibility are considered together. The estimate identifies the lumber treatment and corrosion-resistant hardware, with the applicable code and product instructions guiding the installation.
Ledger, Flashing And Fasteners
At an attached deck, the ledger is where the deck meets the house's wall framing. The code is specific about what goes there.
What The Ledger Attaches To

The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. The band joist behind it must bear fully on the primary structure. DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and cantilevered floors or bay windows. In those cases a non-ledger beam is used instead (Tab 2).
Flashing That Sheds Water

Columbus's deck bulletin requires approved corrosion-resistive flashing wherever a deck attaches to wood-frame construction. DCA 6 specifies metal flashing of at least 0.019-inch nominal thickness, or an approved non-metallic material. It also says aluminum shouldn't touch lumber treated with copper-based preservatives. The door threshold above the deck is flashed and sealed against splash and melting snow.
Lag Screws And Bolts

The drawings identify the fastener type, diameter, spacing and connection details. Ordinary nails and unapproved substitutes cannot replace that connection. Opening the house wall may reveal repairs needed before attachment.
Hardware Rated For Treated Lumber

: hot-dip galvanized fasteners to ASTM A153, or stainless steel, silicon bronze or copper joist hangers and post bases in galvanized (G185) or stainless steel fasteners and connectors of the same corrosion-resistant material, so they don't react with each other.
Boards: Trex And Wood
The boards set the look, the upkeep and the joist spacing. Roof King installs Trex composite and PVC lines as well as cedar and pressure-treated wood.
Upkeep
cleanup for Transcend. Wood is cleaned and inspected regularly. A finish is reapplied if you want to keep the color; unfinished cedar weathers to gray. See deck refinishing for wood upkeep.
Heat In The Sun

Some Trex lines and colors include heat-mitigating technology. They can still become hot, especially darker colors. Compare the selected line’s published heat information and plan shade for exposed seating and walking areas.
How Boards Are Fastened
Hidden fastening leaves no visible screw holes in the walking surface. See Trex Hideaway fasteners.

Guard posts are bolted into the framing, and lighting wires run through posts and rails. Changing either after framing can mean opening finished work. DCA 6 also calls for a light source at stairways. More options: deck railings and accessories.

Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

Almost always. Inside city limits, a deck needs a building permit and plan review. The one exception is a deck of 200 square feet or less that's no more than 30 inches above grade, isn't attached to the house and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval is also required for any deck over 169 square feet.
How deep do deck footings have to be in Columbus?

The approved design must account for local frost depth, soil bearing, deck loads and nearby foundations. Footings are inspected before concrete is placed. A shallow block or an old patio slab is not an automatic substitute for a footing designed for the deck.
Should my deck be attached to the house or freestanding?

It depends on the wall behind it. A ledger-attached deck needs solid band- joist framing and careful flashing. If a positive connection can't be verified, the code requires the deck to be self-supporting. Brick or stone veneer, bay windows and cantilevered floors need a beam on its own posts instead of a ledger.
Can a deck ledger go over brick or stone?

No. The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. AWC's DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and floor overhangs. A non-ledger deck, with an extra beam and posts at the house, is used instead.
How far apart are the joists for Trex decking?
Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when the boards run diagonally. Joist spacing is chosen together with the board line.
Does composite decking get hot?
Yes. Trex says all decking can get hot in direct sun, especially darker colors. Its SunComfortable colors reduced heat buildup by up to 35 degrees compared with Trex's original boards in lab testing.
How tall does a deck railing need to be?

In Columbus, a 36-inch guard is required where the deck is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.
Can I finance a new deck?
Ask our team about current financing for eligible deck projects, then review the lender’s rates, repayment schedule and conditions. Financing is subject to lender approval and applicable terms.

expectedBlocks: A wood deck refinish starts with the boards and the finish already on them. Roof King checks for repairs, prepares the surface and applies a suitable stain to Columbus cedar and pressure-treated decks. We explain the expected color, grain variation and drying requirements before the work begins.
Plan the Preparation and Finish for Your Wood Deck
Check whether the deck needs refinishing, compare stain types and understand the preparation and weather conditions that affect the result. Composite boards follow a different care plan.
Does It Need Refinishing?
Wood decks give clear signs when the finish has stopped protecting them. Look for water soaking in, graying, and rough or checked boards. You can check the first two yourself in a few minutes.
Planning and Installation Details
The Splash Test

Water beads and runs off: the finish is still repelling water. Water darkens the wood and soaks in: the finish has worn through, and the deck is due for refinishing. The Forest Products Laboratory describes this test for water-repellent finishes, and Cabot uses the same check for stains: if the stain still repels water, it's still working. On a new deck, the same test tells you when the wood is ready to take stain. If the droplets soak in, it can be stained.
Gray Or Blotchy Boards

research explains that unfinished wood outdoors loses its surface color and picks up mildew, so all species eventually turn gray. It treats graying on a finished deck as a sign the finish needs renewing. Cleaning removes the gray layer before new stain goes on.
Rough, Checked Or Splintering Boards

Surface checks are common on deck boards because the sun dries the top of the board faster than the rest. Sanding can take the loose, weathered fibers off before a new finish. A board that is soft, split through, cupped badly or loose at its fasteners needs repair or replacement first. Stain does not fix wood that has lost strength. See deck repair.
Peeling Or Flaking Finish
next coat New stain over a peeling film peels with it. Loose finish has to come off before the deck is refinished, and the estimate says how.
References for This Topic

Requirements apply to the property’s jurisdiction and the selected product. City of Columbus Deck and Egress Requirements · Ohio Residential Code: Floor and Deck Construction · Cabot Deck Staining Guidance
Stain Types
Deck stains run from nearly clear to fully opaque. More pigment hides more of the wood. On a surface people walk on, though, more pigment also means more film that can wear and peel.
Clear And Toned (Transparent) Finishes

Newer or well-kept cedar and decks where you want the natural wood to show Penetrating water-repellent finishes are one of the finish types the Forest Products Laboratory recommends for fully exposed decks. They also wear fastest: FPL notes that a water-repellent preservative used as a natural finish may last only 1 to 2 years. Renewing it is simple: clean, then recoat.
Semi-Transparent Stain

Most weathered wood decks, including pressure-treated pine Penetrating semi-transparent stains soak into the wood instead of forming a film, so they don't blister or peel. When it's time to recoat, heavy scraping and sanding usually aren't needed. They have to soak in to work. Excess that sits on the surface is wiped off rather than left to form shiny spots.
Semi-Solid Stain
uneven weathering where you still want some texture to show.
Solid-Color Stain

Solid-color stains form a film much like paint. The Forest Products Laboratory warns that, unless a product is specially formulated for decks, they shouldn't be used on horizontal surfaces because they lack abrasion resistance and tend to flake. Going back from a solid stain to a semi-transparent one means removing the old film, because a penetrating stain can't soak through it. If a solid look is what you want, we choose a product labeled for deck floors and show you how it will need to be maintained.
Explore the Product Options
Cedar Decking
Pressure-Treated Decking
Preparation
Most of a refinish happens before any stain is opened. Repairs, cleaning and the right amount of stripping or sanding decide how evenly the stain soaks in and how long it lasts.
Repairs Approved First

How we handle it We point out each problem during the visit and price it separately. Repair work starts only after you approve it. A new board will look different from weathered boards at first, and we tell you that up front. Structural problems such as posts, framing and stairs are handled through deck repair.
Cleaning

The cleaner and the pressure used have to suit the wood and the stain going on. Cleaning that is too aggressive can raise and tear soft wood. After cleaning, the deck needs time to dry. Cabot, for example, calls for a rinse and two to three days of drying before staining.
Stripping Or Sanding

each is used Stripping: loose, peeling or incompatible finish, or when switching from a solid stain to a semi-transparent one. Sanding: rough, fuzzy or splintering boards, and spots where old finish remains. A well-kept penetrating stain may only need cleaning before a fresh coat. The estimate states which method we'll use, and which finish, if any, stays on.
Protecting The House And Yard
cover Nearby siding, the house foundation, plantings and hard surfaces get covered or protected, and we clean up when the work is done.
Weather And Timing

Stain needs the right temperature and dry wood on both the day it goes on and the night after. In central Ohio, spring and fall afternoons can feel warm enough while the boards are still cold or damp from the night, so we plan around the wood as well as the forecast.
Air And Board Temperature
Cabot gives 50–90°F for its general deck-staining guidance. The coating’s own label controls the job; direct sun can make the boards much hotter than the forecast air temperature.
Rain And Dew

Manufacturers call for a rain-free window after application. Cabot asks for a day with no rain expected for 24 hours, and notes that wet or cold weather can double drying time. We check the National Weather Service's hourly forecast for your address, including overnight temperature, dew point and rain chances.
Drying Time After Cleaning

Cleaning and staining may need separate visits. The gap depends on wood moisture, shade, ventilation and weather; Cabot’s general guidance allows two to three days of drying after washing. We confirm readiness before coating.
Staining A Brand-New Deck
example, recommends waiting 4 to 8 weeks after a new deck is built, then using the water-drop test. Planning a new deck? See deck installation.
Composite Decks

Composite boards like Trex are not stained or sanded. The care they need is cleaning, and the right method depends on the product line. If your composite deck looks tired, the fix is a proper cleaning, replacing damaged boards, or a new surface.
Transcend, Enhance And Select

Trex's limits A pressure washer should not exceed 3100 psi, must use a fan tip, and should be held no closer than 8 inches to the surface. Rinse thoroughly so a film of dirty water doesn't dry on the boards.
Older Trex Lines

Hose off debris, then scrub with warm soapy water and a soft-bristle brush. Trex recommends a composite deck cleaner twice a year. Trex says not to pressure wash these lines, because it can damage the surface and void the warranty.
No Sanding, No Metal Shovels

"Trex does not recommend sanding." It changes the surface appearance and voids the warranty for related conditions. Never use a metal snow shovel on Trex decking. Trex allows calcium chloride or rock salt for ice. For a line not listed here, such as Refuge, follow that line's own care guide.
When Cleaning Isn't Enough

How do I know if my deck needs refinishing?

Splash some water on the boards. If it beads up, the finish is still working. If the wood darkens and soaks it up, or the deck has turned gray, it's time to refinish. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory and stain maker Cabot both describe this check.
Can a new stain go over the old one?
Sometimes. A sound penetrating stain can often be cleaned and recoated with a compatible product. A peeling finish, or a solid stain you want to swap for a semi-transparent, has to come off first.
Is a semi-transparent or solid stain better for a deck?

For most wood decks, a semi-transparent stain lasts better underfoot because it soaks in instead of forming a film that can peel. A solid stain hides more, but use one only if it's made for deck floors.
What weather do you need to stain a deck in Columbus?

The boards must be dry, air and surface temperatures must fit the selected coating’s label, and the forecast must provide its required drying window. Cabot’s general deck guidance gives 50–90°F; individual finishes can have different rain, dew and curing requirements.
How soon can we use the deck after staining?

Dry-to-touch, foot-traffic and furniture times can differ. We provide the selected coating’s instructions and allow for the actual weather rather than promising one return-to-use time for every finish.
Can you stain or sand a Trex deck?
No. Trex composite gets cleaned, not stained, and Trex doesn't recommend sanding. Its care page gives pressure-washing limits for its newer lines and says not to pressure wash the older ones.
Do I need a permit to refinish my deck in Columbus?

The City of Columbus lists exterior painting among the projects that don't need a permit, and staining isn't listed separately. Building a deck does need a permit and plan review. Historic or special districts may need other approvals.
Will refinishing hide replaced boards and old marks?
Not completely. New boards, weathering and grain differences can still show after staining. A semi-solid or solid stain evens out color more, and we go over the expected look before work begins.

expectedBlocks: A soft board, moving rail or sagging stair can point to damage beyond the visible surface. Roof King assesses deck boards, framing and connections in Columbus, then explains whether a targeted repair, resurfacing or replacement fits. Keep people off areas that appear unstable until they have been assessed.
Find the Deck Component That Needs Attention
Choose the damaged area to see what we check, how repairs connect to the surrounding structure and when a larger replacement becomes the more useful comparison.
Boards And Fasteners
A board that is soft, split or cupped can sometimes be swapped on its own. First we check the joists under it and the fasteners holding it, because a new board on wet framing will fail again.
Planning and Installation Details
Soft Or Spongy Boards

How we check it We probe the board and the framing under it. NADRA's checklist says that if a tool easily sinks ¼–½ inch, or the wood is soft and spongy, decay may be present. We look at the joist tops under the board, where water collects. If decay reaches the joists, the fix includes the framing, not just the board.
Split, Cupped Or Popped Boards

repair involves Replacing the damaged length with a board of compatible thickness and width so it sits flush Ending cuts over a joist so each board end has support Refastening the surrounding boards where nails have backed out
Rusted Screws, Nails And Connectors

Corroded screws and nails in the deck surface Rusted joist hangers, post bases and other connectors we can reach For Trex boards, the fastening system that fits the board profile, such as Hideaway clips or face screws
References for This Topic

Requirements apply to the property’s jurisdiction and the selected product. City of Columbus Deck and Egress Requirements · Ohio Residential Code: Floor and Deck Construction · Trex Installation and Care Resources
Framing, Ledger And Flashing

The joists, beams and ledger carry the deck. The ledger is the board bolted to the house, and NADRA calls it "a common source of deck failure." That's why we check it on every repair visit where it can be reached.
Ledger Attachment

Columbus requires and what we look for City of Columbus guidance (Residential Code of Ohio 502.2.2) says an attached deck must resist vertical and horizontal movement and may not rely on toenails or nails subject to withdrawal. NADRA's checklist says the ledger should not be fastened with only nails. We look for missing or rusted bolts, crushed or rotted wood at the ledger, and a gap opening between the deck and the house.
Ledger Flashing

Columbus guidance (RCO 703.8) requires corrosion-resistant flashing where a deck attaches to a wood-frame wall, so water can't enter the wall cavity or reach the structure. Missing or failed flashing can rot the ledger and the house rim joist behind it. Fixing that may mean removing boards near the house and opening the siding at the deck line. We note in the estimate when the wall behind the ledger can only be judged once it is opened.
Joists And Beams

options we'll discuss Replacing a decayed joist or beam section where the surrounding framing is sound Replacing failed hangers and connectors When decay runs across many joists, a deck replacement is usually the sounder plan (see the "Repair or replace" tab)
Posts And Footings

A deck that sways, sags or has one low corner often has a problem at a post or footing. NADRA's checklist says a deck or stair should look even, without sagging, and should not sway or move when tested.
Post Bases

repair can involve Replacing a decayed post while the beam is temporarily supported Replacing rusted post bases and beam connectors Using lumber rated for its exposure. Ground-contact members can need a different treatment rating than deck boards
Settled Or Cracked Footings

The post can only be as stable as the footing under it. A failed footing may need replacing before the post is reset. Footing work on a deck that serves a door or sits above 30 inches can fall under the city's permit rules (see the "Permits in Columbus" tab).
Sway And Bounce
Common causes Loose or under-fastened ledger Missing bracing or loose beam-to-post connections Undersized or decayed joists
Stairs And Railings

Stairs and railings are where people put their weight and hands, so we check every connection, not just the tread or baluster that looks worn. NADRA's checklist calls for railings and handrails to be firmly held in place, and for risers and stringers to be securely attached and free of decay.
Stair Stringers And Treads

Columbus stair dimensions (City guidance on RCO 311.7.4) Risers no more than 8¼ inches high, treads not less than 9 inches Open risers allowed if a 4-inch sphere can't pass between treads Solid risers need a nosing of ¾ inch to 1¼ inches
Handrails
Steps with 4 or more risers need a handrail on at least one side, 34 to 38 inches high (RCO 311.7.7).
Guards (Deck Railings)

What we check Columbus guidance (RCO 312.1) calls for a 36-inch guard on decks where the grade is more than 30 inches below the deck surface, measured 3 feet out from the edge. Railing posts and their attachment to the rim joist Replacing a damaged railing section with a compatible system. For new railing styles, see deck railings and accessories
Repair Or Replace

Repair makes sense when the problem is limited and what stays is sound. Once the framing or ledger has broad damage, a deck replacement, or resurfacing over framing that is still sound, is usually a better plan than one repair after another. We'll show you what we found so you can make the call.
A Targeted Repair Fits When…
enough Decay is limited to isolated boards or one or two framing members The ledger, flashing and footings check out Replacement parts are available in a compatible size and material
Consider Resurfacing When…

New boards over existing framing only work if the framing meets the new product's requirements. Trex lists pressure-treated lumber or steel as its recommended substructure. Resurfacing and full replacement are planned on our deck replacement and resurfacing page
Plan A Replacement When…

Decay across many joists, the ledger or several posts A ledger that was nailed on or never flashed, with damage behind it Repairs that would rebuild most of the deck anyway You want a different size or layout. See deck replacement or new deck installation
Matching Your Deck

New boards and rails rarely look identical to old ones at first. Wood weathers, and product colors and lines change over time. Even Trex says its early-generation composites "did fade slightly" as they weathered. We bring samples and point out any visible difference before you choose a selective repair.
Refinish After The Repair, Not Before
Finish structural and board repairs first, then plan deck refinishing for wood decks. Trex says painting or staining its decking is not recommended and may void the fade and stain warranty.

Permits In Columbus

Many small fixes, such as swapping a few boards, don't change how a deck is built. Work on the parts that carry people out of the house is different. City of Columbus Building and Zoning Services requires plan approval and building permits for alterations to the means of egress between the exit door and the ground, including landings, decks, ramps and stairs.
The One Exception

200 square feet or less Not more than 30 inches above grade at any point Not attached to the house Not serving the required exit door Zoning approval is still required for any deck over 169 square feet, whatever its location or height.
Low Stairs And Landings
Building A Deck

Also check Historic districts and area commissions (for example German Village) may need extra approvals before work starts. Outside Columbus city limits, your own city or village building department sets the rules. Ask about permit requirements when you review your estimate.
Safety Checks Behind Every Deck Repair Estimate
Where the Deck Meets the House

We assess the ledger, attachment and flashing, then look for deterioration or water staining at the adjoining wall. A house-connection problem changes the repair and needs to be identified before the estimate focuses only on surface boards.
Damage Where Boards Meet the Stairs

Split or decayed board ends beside a step need assessment of the support and fasteners underneath, not simply a new surface board. We check the adjoining joists, stringers and connections and describe supporting repairs separately from finishing.
Where People Step and Hold On

Stair treads, stringers, handrails and guard posts take concentrated loads during everyday use. We assess their connections as well as the visible parts and identify whether the repair needs supporting framing or blocking.

Your written estimate identifies the materials, preparation, construction and cleanup so you can compare the same work between proposals.

Replacement lumber or Trex line, fasteners and connectors
Ledger, flashing, hangers, post bases and adjoining wall work
Retained components and access needed below the boards
Disposal, cleanup and separately listed refinishing
How hidden deterioration is documented and approved
What Changes the Price
Size, height, access, demolition, retained versus new structure, materials, stairs and railing length all affect the price. A deck-area rate alone does not describe those differences.
Additional Repairs and Scheduling

If opening the deck reveals further deterioration, we document it and explain the added repair before it is approved. Material lead times, permit review and weather affect scheduling; the proposal identifies the planned work and responsibilities.
Do I need a permit to repair my deck in Columbus?

It depends on what the repair changes. City of Columbus guidance requires plan approval and permits for alterations to the exit path from the house, which includes landings, decks and stairs. The only exception is a deck that is 200 sq ft or less, no more than 30 inches above grade, freestanding and not serving the required exit door. Low stairs and landings can be issued a minor permit that needs a final inspection.
Can you replace just the damaged boards?
Often, yes, if the joists under them are sound. We check the framing first, and the work area can grow if we need access below. Some color difference between new and weathered boards is normal.
How do I know if my deck is safe to use?

Warning signs include soft wood, boards or stairs that sag, a deck that sways, loose railings, rusted connectors, and a gap where the deck meets the house. NADRA recommends a professional evaluation, and if you notice any of these, keep people off that area until it's checked.
What is a ledger board, and why does it matter?

It's the board that attaches the deck to your house. NADRA calls it a common source of deck failure. Columbus requires attached decks to resist vertical and horizontal movement without relying on nails that can pull out, plus corrosion-resistant flashing at the wall.
Can new composite boards go on my existing framing?

Only when the framing is sound and meets the product's requirements. Trex lists pressure-treated lumber or steel as its recommended substructure, and spacing and condition need checking before resurfacing. See deck replacement and resurfacing.
A storm or tree limb damaged my deck. What should I do?

Keep everyone off it, photograph the damage from a safe position, and contact your insurer about its reporting process. Then call us to look at the deck along with any other exterior damage. Our estimate describes the damage and the repair; it doesn't decide a claim.
Should I stain or seal before or after repairs?

After. Fix the boards and framing first so a new finish doesn't hide a problem, then plan deck refinishing for wood decks. For Trex boards, Trex says painting or staining isn't recommended and may void the fade and stain warranty.

expectedBlocks: Worn boards can hide a sound frame or a structure that needs rebuilding. Roof King checks the ledger, joists, posts and footings before recommending resurfacing or full deck replacement in Columbus. The estimate names what stays, what comes off and how the new boards, railings and stairs are built.
Decide What Stays and What Needs Replacing
Use the condition of the structure to compare resurfacing with a rebuild, then consider layout improvements and the materials for the new surface.
Signs It's Time To Replace

A deck needs replacing when the problems reach the parts that hold it up: the ledger, posts, footings, joists and railing connections. Damage limited to a few boards or one loose rail is a repair. For that, see deck repair. Age catches up with decks everywhere. NADRA, the North American Deck and Railing Association, estimates that about 30 million of the 60 million decks in the U.S. have outlived their useful life.
Planning and Installation Details
Rot In The Frame, Not Just The Boards

Joist ends and the tops of joists, where water sits under the boards The ledger and the house rim joist behind it Beam ends and post tops, where wood meets wood Posts at grade, especially where soil or mulch is piled against them Decay in one board is a repair. Decay in several joists or at the ledger usually means rebuilding rather than resurfacing. NADRA's consumer checklist names decaying materials as a key warning sign.
A Loose Or Poorly Attached Ledger

ledger looks like Columbus's deck bulletin says an attached deck must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and it can't be attached with toenails or nails that can pull out. The American Wood Council's deck guide (DCA 6) calls for ½-inch lag screws or bolts and corrosion-resistant flashing at the wall. It prohibits fastening a ledger to brick veneer, hollow masonry or a cantilevered floor overhang. Warning signs: A gap opening between the ledger and the house A ledger held with nails only Missing or rusted flashing above the ledger Water stains or soft wood on the house framing below it Fixing a ledger properly means taking up the boards along the house, which is often the point where a full replacement makes more sense.
Failing Posts And Footings

What current practice calls for DCA 6 prescribes posts of at least 6x6. The beam must sit on a notched post or a post cap, not be bolted to the side of the post. Footings bear on undisturbed soil at least 12 inches below grade or below the frost line, whichever is deeper. Many older decks have 4x4 posts, beams bolted to the side of the posts, or shallow pier blocks. New boards don't change any of that; correcting it means rebuilding the substructure.
Soft, Springy Or Split Boards Across The Deck

Boards or joists? One soft board is a repair. Widespread bounce usually traces to joists spaced too far apart for the boards, or to joist tops that have started to decay. Measure the joist spacing before choosing new boards. Composite needs closer spacing than many older wood decks were built with (see tab 3, "Upgrade from wood to Trex composite").
Railings And Stairs That Move

What Columbus requires A 36-inch guard wherever the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge A handrail 34–38 inches high on at least one side of any stair with 4 or more risers Stair risers no higher than 8¼ inches, treads at least 9 inches deep, and openings that won't pass a 4-inch sphere DCA 6 calls for guard posts of at least 4x4, bolted to joists or a rim of at least 2x8 and secured with hold-down hardware rated for 1,800 pounds. Railing posts depend on the frame. When the frame is replaced, the railing usually is too. Compare railing systems on deck railings and accessories.
Rusted Hardware And Dark Stairs

Why the metal matters DCA 6 requires hot-dip galvanized or stainless steel fasteners and connectors with preservative-treated lumber. Rusted joist hangers, ledger bolts and post bases lose capacity long before they break. DCA 6 also calls for a light at the top landing that lights every stair, switched from inside the house. A replacement is the time to correct both.
References for This Topic

Requirements apply to the property’s jurisdiction and the selected product. City of Columbus Deck and Egress Requirements · Ohio Residential Code: Floor and Deck Construction · Trex Installation and Care Resources
Resurface Or Replace The Whole Deck

Roof King offers both resurfacing and full replacement. Resurfacing keeps the existing frame and replaces what you walk on and touch: the boards, and usually the railings, stair treads and fascia. Full replacement removes the deck and rebuilds the structure. The frame decides which one fits your deck, not the condition of the old boards. Fixing a few named parts on a deck that stays is deck repair.
Compare the Work Included
When Resurfacing Makes Sense

Resurfacing usually works when… Joists, beams and ledger are dry and solid, with no decay at the ends or along the ledger The ledger is bolted to the house and flashed Posts and footings meet the practice described in tab 1 Joist spacing suits the new boards, or can be corrected by adding joists You're happy with the current size, shape and stair location The estimate names every retained component, and any repair found once the old boards are off is documented and approved before it's covered.
When A Full Replacement Is The Better Call

Plan a full replacement when… Decay runs through several joists, the beam or the ledger The ledger is nailed, or attached to brick veneer or a floor overhang Posts are undersized or footings are shallow You want a different size, height or shape, or the stairs need to move A changed footprint is a design job. Our deck installation page covers layout, access and the supporting construction for a new design.
What Resurfacing Still Involves

old surface exposes the joist tops, hangers and ledger for the first time in years. That's when the frame is checked closely. Rusted hardware is replaced, weak joists are reinforced or replaced, and added joists go in if the new boards need closer spacing. Railings and stairs are usually renewed at the same time, because their posts and stringers attach to the frame.
Comparing A Resurfacing Price With A Replacement Price

Ask for both when the frame is borderline A resurfacing proposal should list each retained component and its condition. A replacement proposal should list the new footings, posts, beams, joists and ledger. Where the frame could go either way, ask for both options priced side by side. That way a lower surface-only price isn't mistaken for a rebuilt deck.
Upgrade From Wood To Trex Composite

A replacement is the best time to change materials, because the frame is open and can be set up for the new boards. Roof King's product library covers Trex decking, railing and accessories, along with cedar and pressure-treated wood for homeowners who want to stay with wood.
Upkeep: Composite Vs Wood

What each material asks of you Trex describes soap-and-water cleanup for Transcend. Roof King's product pages list periodic cleaning and no routine wood staining for the Trex lines, with methods that depend on the line. Composite isn't maintenance-free: leaves in the board gaps hold moisture against the frame, and drainage still needs checking. Wood decks need a finish system and renewal, which is our deck refinishing service.
Can Trex Go On My Existing Frame?

joist spacing first Trex says joists for its decking should generally be no more than 16 inches on center. Diagonal boards need 12 inches, and heavier loads, longer spans or patterns can need 12 inches or less. Older wood decks were sometimes framed at 24 inches. Trex's fix is one new joist between each existing pair. Add-in joists can't make up for decay, a poor ledger or weak footings (see tab 1). Each board also needs its own fasteners and edge details for the line selected.
Heat In Summer Sun

Some Trex lines and colors include heat-mitigating technology. They can still become hot, especially darker colors. Compare the selected line’s published heat information and plan shade for exposed seating and walking areas.
Two Warranties, Two Jobs

covers what Trex's limited residential warranties cover the product and differ by line. Transcend and Transcend Lineage carry 50-year limited residential warranties; Select carries a 35-year and Enhance a 25-year limited residential fade-and-stain warranty. Roof King's 5-year workmanship warranty covers our installation and is separate from the manufacturer's terms. Keep both documents with your project records.

Tear-Out, Permits And Code
A replacement starts with taking the old deck apart. Inside Columbus city limits, rebuilding a deck is permitted work with plan review.
Tear-Out And Disposal

removal covers Which parts come off: boards, railings, stairs, framing, and whether the footings stay or go How debris is collected and hauled away What is protected: plantings, the door threshold and the siding along the house How a condition found after removal, such as rot in the house rim joist, is documented and approved before it's covered DCA 6 requires removing the siding at the ledger before a new ledger goes on, adding flashing, and carefully flashing and caulking the door threshold. As a siding contractor too, Roof King can handle the wall details where the deck meets the house.
Columbus Permits For A Replacement Deck

city's documents say The city's deck bulletin (revised April 3, 2026) requires plan approval and building permits for decks, stairs and landings between the exit door and the ground. The only exception is a deck of no more than 200 square feet that is no more than 30 inches above grade at any point, isn't attached to the house and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval is required for any deck over 169 square feet, whatever its height or location. Landings and stairs no more than 30 inches above grade may be issued a minor limited permit and need a final inspection. In a special zoning district, area commission or historic district (German Village or the University Overlay, for example), more approvals may be needed before work starts. The city's documents don't list board-only resurfacing separately, so the permit path for a resurfacing is confirmed for your address. Addresses outside Columbus city limits follow their own building department. Your estimate states who applies for the permit and schedules inspections.
Code Details The New Deck Must Meet

The step down from the door to the deck: no more than 8¼ inches when the door doesn't swing out over the deck Stair risers no higher than 8¼ inches and treads at least 9 inches deep; open risers may not pass a 4-inch sphere A 34–38 inch handrail on stairs with 4 or more risers A 36-inch guard where the deck is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out An attached deck that resists vertical and horizontal movement, with no toenails or nails subject to withdrawal Corrosion-resistant flashing where the deck attaches to a wood-frame wall
Footings And Buried Utilities

Below the deck DCA 6 places footings on undisturbed soil at least 12 inches deep or below the frost line, whichever is deeper. Deck footings within 5 feet of the house foundation must bear at the same depth as the house footing. Footings never go over septic systems, utility lines or enclosed meters. Utilities are located (contact the appropriate public agency) before digging. Where existing footings are kept, the estimate says so.
What Changes Beneath a Replacement Deck
Frame, Ledger and Footings

A full rebuild addresses the supporting structure as well as the boards. For resurfacing, the same footings, posts, beams, joists and house connection need to be checked for condition and compatibility before new material covers them.
Keep the Footprint or Improve the Layout

The door, stair landing and usable seating area determine whether the existing footprint still works. A different shape or height changes the framing and approvals; retaining the old outline does not remove the need to assess its supports.
New Boards and Railings Need Suitable Supports

A new Trex surface or railing must fit the retained frame’s spacing and attachment points. Added joists, blocking, post repairs and edge finishing belong in the estimate so the visible upgrade is supported correctly.
What Your Deck Replacement Estimate Includes
Your written estimate identifies the materials, preparation, construction and cleanup so you can compare the same work between proposals.
Removal, disposal and protection of the house and yard
Each retained and new footing, post, beam, joist and ledger
House attachment, flashing and additional joists or blocking
Board line, color, fasteners and fascia
Railings, stairs, handrails and selected accessories
Permit and inspection responsibilities, cleanup and warranty documents
What Changes the Price
Size, height, access, demolition, retained versus new structure, materials, stairs and railing length all affect the price. A deck-area rate alone does not describe those differences.
Additional Repairs and Scheduling

If opening the deck reveals further deterioration, we document it and explain the added repair before it is approved. Material lead times, permit review and weather affect scheduling; the proposal identifies the planned work and responsibilities.
Do I need a permit to replace my deck in Columbus?

For a rebuild, yes. Inside city limits, building a deck requires a permit and plan review. The only exception is a deck of no more than 200 square feet that is no more than 30 inches above grade, isn't attached to the house and doesn't serve the required exit door. Board-only resurfacing isn't listed separately in the city's documents, so its permit path is confirmed for your address. Outside the city, your local building department sets the rules.
Is resurfacing cheaper than a full replacement?

Usually, because the footings, posts and frame stay. But that only holds if the frame is sound. A resurfacing that has to add joists, replace a ledger and repair several joists can approach the cost of a rebuild. That's why we price both when the frame is borderline.
Will my new deck need new footings?

If the existing footings are too shallow, too small or were poured for posts in different places, yes. Footings must bear on undisturbed soil at least 12 inches deep or below the frost line, whichever is deeper. Footings that meet the requirement and suit the new layout can stay, and the estimate says so.
Can you keep my existing railing or stairs?

Only if they're solid and fit the new deck. Railing posts and stair stringers attach to the frame, so a rebuilt frame usually means new ones. The new railing must meet Columbus's guard and handrail heights. Railing choices are covered on deck railings and accessories.
What happens to my old deck?
Taking it apart and hauling it away is part of the replacement. The estimate lists what comes off, how debris is removed and what is protected while we work.
Can the new deck be a different size?
Yes. A different size or shape changes the footings, framing, stairs and approvals, so it's planned as a new design. See new deck installation for layout questions.
Does a composite deck still need maintenance?

Less than wood, but some. Trex describes soap-and-water cleanup. Keep the board gaps clear of leaves so moisture doesn't sit on the frame, and check the drainage and the ledger area after storms. A wood deck needs its finish renewed; see deck refinishing.
Can I finance a deck replacement?
Ask our team about current financing for eligible deck projects, then review the lender’s rates, repayment schedule and conditions. Financing is subject to lender approval and applicable terms.

children.text: If you’re planning roofing, siding or exterior work in Delaware, the useful starting point is the condition of the surfaces being repaired—not a package selected before an inspection.

sections.title: Coordinating roofing, siding and storm repairs in Delaware

children.text: The details that deserve particular attention at your Delaware property include: entry roofs, masonry connections and older-to-newer building transitions. When more than one exterior area needs work, identifying these connections early helps coordinate materials and installation.
When roofing and siding work should be coordinated

Where a roof edge meets siding or fascia, a damaged flashing or support detail may affect both projects. Reviewing those junctions together can make the proposed work easier to understand, even if the work is completed in stages.

cards.title: Roof-to-wall details on your Delaware home

children.text: Where a lower roof meets siding, the flashing belongs in the repair plan for both surfaces. Replacing one finish should not leave a failed connection hidden behind the other. We discuss the repair sequence so roofing and wall work meet correctly.

New roofing and siding can meet the same fascia boards and gutter supports. If those areas are damaged, the preparation should be identified before new materials are fastened. Gutter outlets and downspouts are considered with the route water takes away from the house.

cards.title: Storm repairs across your Delaware exterior

children.text: One storm can affect roofing, siding, trim and drainage differently. Documenting the areas together helps separate the repairs each material needs and coordinate the work around retained surfaces. Construction photos and a written estimate keep those decisions visible.

sections.title: Roofing, siding and storm repair estimates in Delaware

children.text: Your Delaware estimate should identify the areas being repaired or replaced, the materials being removed or retained and the proposed products. Roofing details can include tear-off, deck repairs, underlayment, flashing and ventilation. Siding details can include wall preparation, trim and flashing at openings. Storm repairs should identify the affected surfaces rather than rely on a general damage description.

Delivery, access, cleanup and how additional concealed repairs are approved also belong in the written plan. Product and workmanship coverage are separate; the applicable written terms should identify the protection for your installation.

sections.title: When Should You Replace Your Gutters?

children.text: Not every drip means the whole system needs replacement. An isolated joint or outlet may be repairable when the surrounding gutter and support are still sound. But widespread sagging, recurring overflow, corrosion, loose attachment or repeated leaks at several locations can make replacement the more practical choice.

Pay attention to water staining on siding, peeling paint near the roof edge, washed-out landscaping and water pooling next to the house. These symptoms do not always begin at the gutter. cards.title: Downspouts and Drainage Away From the House

Not every drip means the whole system needs replacement. An isolated joint or outlet may be repairable when the surrounding gutter and support are still sound. How do I know whether to repair or replace my gutters?

A localized joint, outlet or hanger issue may be repairable. Multiple failing sections, corrosion, widespread sagging or damaged supporting materials can make replacement more sensible. The condition of the existing system matters more than its age alone.
Are seamless gutters completely leak-free?
No. Seamless construction reduces joints along straight runs, but corners, end caps and outlets still require connections. Installation details and maintenance remain important.
Will larger gutters stop overflowing?
Not necessarily. Blocked outlets, poor slope, insufficient downspout capacity or discharge problems can still cause overflow. The whole drainage route needs to be evaluated.
Do gutter guards eliminate cleaning?
No. Guards can reduce certain debris entry, but the gutter, outlets and downspouts still need inspection and maintenance according to the product instructions.
Can gutters be installed when fascia is damaged?
Damaged fascia or other roof-edge support may need repair first. The estimate should identify that work or explain how concealed damage will be handled.

Gutters are fastened to the edge of a building where roofing, fascia, soffit and siding meet. If the support is deteriorated, attaching new gutters over it can leave a weak connection. Water behind a gutter can also be confused with a roof leak.

Are seamless gutters completely leak-proof?
No. They reduce joints along straight runs, but corners, end caps and outlets still need connections. Good installation and routine maintenance remain important.
Will seamless gutters stop overflowing?
Only if the cause is addressed. The gutter size, roof runoff, outlets, downspouts and discharge route all affect overflow.
Can a damaged seamless gutter be repaired?
Sometimes. The location and extent of damage, material and connections determine whether a localized repair or replacement of a run makes more sense.
Are seamless gutters available in different colors?
Color and finish options depend on the material and profile available for the project. Ask to see the actual choices included in the estimate.
Do seamless gutters need cleaning?
Yes. Leaves and debris can still collect in the gutter or at outlets. Follow the care instructions for the selected system and inspect areas that overflow.
Can I add gutter guards at the same time?
Often, yes, provided the guard is compatible with the gutter and roof edge. Review the selected guard's installation and maintenance requirements.
Does Roof King offer financing for gutter installation?
Roof King provides financing information for eligible projects. Availability and terms depend on lender approval and the current offer. Ask for the written details.

How to Recognize an Ice Dam

Icicles by themselves do not prove that a roof has an ice dam. Look for a solid ridge of ice at the eaves with snow or meltwater sitting above it. Water stains, damp insulation and active leaks near outside walls are warning signs of water entry.
Uneven snow melt can be another clue. If snow disappears from the upper roof while a thick frozen band remains at the edge, heat escaping into the attic may be warming the roof deck.
Signs worth reporting when you contact Roof King:
Ice forming in a continuous band along the roof edge or in a valley.
Ceiling stains, damp drywall or dripping near an exterior wall.
Water behind the fascia, or gutters pulling away under the weight of ice.
Repeated ice buildup on the same roof section after snowstorms.
Why Snow Melts and Refreezes at the Eaves

Snow on a warmer part of the roof melts and flows downhill. When that water reaches the colder eave, it freezes again. Repeated melting and freezing can build a thick ridge of ice along the roof edge.

Warm air leaking into an attic, insulation gaps and some roof or ventilation conditions can warm the upper roof while the eaves remain below freezing. Weather and sun exposure can also affect the pattern.
How Water Backs Up Beneath the Shingles

As the ridge grows, it blocks normal runoff and creates a pocket of meltwater behind it. Water backed up against that barrier can reach gaps or vulnerable details beneath the roof covering. A roof does not have to sink or sag for this to happen.

Clogged gutters can add drainage problems, but clean gutters alone do not prevent ice dams. Ice can form on roofs without gutters, so gutter replacement or guards may leave the underlying cause untouched.
Where Ice Dam Leaks Can Appear

Water beneath the roof covering can wet the roof deck and attic insulation, then travel into ceilings or down an exterior wall. A stain indoors may appear away from the roof entry point. The affected roof edge and the path of the water both need assessment.
What to Do While Ice Is Building Up

Keep people and pets away from heavy icicles or hanging ice. If water is entering the home, move belongings away from the leak where it is safe and document the visible damage. Avoid areas where water is near wiring or electrical fixtures and seek appropriate emergency assistance.

Do not climb onto a snowy or icy roof to chip at the buildup. Sharp tools can damage shingles and flashing. Avoid pressure washers, open flames and improvised heating methods; arrange a professional roof assessment instead.
