Can ice dams cause roof leaks?
Yes. Meltwater can collect behind the frozen ridge and reach vulnerable areas beneath the roof covering. Water stains near outside walls, damp insulation and ceiling drips can indicate water entry.
Will cleaning my gutters stop ice dams?
Not by itself. Gutters need normal maintenance, but ice dams involve uneven roof temperatures and refreezing meltwater. They can form even where gutters are absent.
Is it safe to knock ice off the roof?
No. Climbing onto an icy roof and striking the ice can cause serious injury and damage the roof. Keep clear of unstable buildup and arrange a professional assessment.
How is ice dam removal planned for my roof?

Roof material, slope, ice thickness, access and active water backup determine the removal plan. The assessment identifies the affected area and precautions for the shingles, flashing and gutters, with any follow-up repairs addressed separately.
Does removing an ice dam fix a ceiling leak?
Removal may relieve the water backup, but damage to the roof, insulation or interior finishes still needs evaluation. A separate repair may be necessary after the ice clears.
Will insurance pay for ice dam damage?

Coverage depends on your policy, the cause of the damage and the insurer’s determination. Document the visible damage from a safe position and contact your insurer about the reporting process. Roof King’s assessment and estimate describe the roofing work; the insurer determines coverage.
Can gutter guards prevent ice dams?
Gutter guards can reduce certain debris problems. They do not control attic heat loss or guarantee that ice will not form at the roof edge.

Common roof repairs in Dublin
The right repair depends on which part of the roof has failed and what is happening around it. These are common areas we inspect when a roof leaks or shows visible damage.
Missing or damaged shingles

A limited area of missing, lifted or damaged shingles may be repairable when the surrounding roof is sound. The repair needs to account for the layers beneath the shingles and how the new material connects to the existing roof. Available products and weathering affect how closely the repair will match.
Pipe boots and roof vents

The flashing around a plumbing vent helps keep water out where the pipe passes through the roof. A split collar, damaged boot or poorly integrated flashing can leave an opening even when nearby shingles look fine. The inspection checks that connection and the surrounding roofing together.
Chimney and wall flashing

Where a roof meets a chimney, wall or dormer, flashing directs water across the transition. Loose pieces, damaged joints or poorly connected layers can let water behind the roof covering. A repair may involve exposing the connection and replacing the affected flashing and adjacent materials.
Valleys and roof edges

Valleys carry runoff from adjoining roof slopes. Roof edges connect the covering with the fascia and gutters. Damage, debris or an incomplete connection in these areas can change where water goes. Identifying the cause helps determine whether the work belongs in the roof, the drainage system or both.

Step flashing carries water down the roof beside the masonry or wall. The wall-side protection and the shingles must connect with it. A smear of sealant over an exposed joint does not explain whether those layered connections have been restored.
Roof repair or replacement: what the inspection changes

An isolated failure in a serviceable roof can be a reasonable repair candidate. Multiple deteriorating areas, repeated unresolved leaks or material that cannot accept a compatible repair may change the decision. Compare roof replacement when the inspection identifies broader problems. A replacement recommendation should explain what a repair would leave unresolved.
What a Columbus roof repair estimate should include

Height, slope, access, the size of the working area and product availability affect the repair price. Damage below the covering can add work once exposed. Compare the defined work and additional-work terms, not only the total. A replacement calculator cannot establish the cause or price of a particular leak.
Send Roof King the property address, a description of the problem and any useful repair history. If broader work becomes necessary, the roofing materials guide can help you compare the next options.
What if water is coming in now?

Call to discuss the situation and current availability. Explain which areas are affected and when the leak began. If it followed a storm, see storm damage services for the assessment and records involved.
Can only part of the roof be repaired?
Sometimes. The surrounding material needs to remain serviceable and the new work must connect properly to it. The inspection establishes whether that is practical for the affected area.
Will a repair have a warranty?

Ask for the written coverage for the agreed work, including the area covered and exclusions. Product coverage and contractor workmanship terms are different, and a repair does not automatically receive a full new-roof warranty.

children.text: Loose, cracked or storm-damaged siding is rarely just a panel problem. Roof King & Restoration is a family-owned siding contractor in Columbus. We repair and replace siding and check the trim, flashing and wall layers behind it, so new cladding is not hiding an unresolved leak. Tell us what you see and we will help you compare a focused repair with a wider replacement.

sections.title: How we assess siding damage

children.text: An inspection separates damage to the siding from a problem behind it. These are the three areas we check.
Call for an inspection when you notice:
Buckled, warped or loose courses, or panels that have slipped out of place
Cracks, holes or broken corners after hail or impact
Exposed housewrap or sheathing where a panel is missing
Staining, soft trim or peeling paint near openings
Gaps at corners or where siding meets the roof
Uneven fading and patches that no longer match
Some signs involve the panel itself; staining near a window can start with failed flashing behind it. The inspection is about finding which.

cards.title: Checking flashing and moisture behind siding

children.text: Loose siding, damaged trim, staining and water near a window can come from different failures. A new panel alone does not repair failed flashing or a gap in the weather barrier. Some areas can only be assessed after removal, so the estimate explains how hidden damage is documented, priced and approved.

cards.title: Matching profile and color on a repair

children.text: A repair needs compatible profile, overlap and thickness as well as a similar color. Compare the panel shape and a physical sample against the existing wall in daylight. Weathering means the same color name may not produce an invisible repair.

children.text: Vinyl is a finished-color panel system. The attachment slots, corners and opening trim need to allow thermal movement, while the water barrier and flashing behind the panels direct moisture outside. Compare the exact profile and any insulated backing rather than treating every vinyl line as equivalent.

LP SmartSide offers engineered-wood lap, panel, shake and trim profiles. Sealed cut edges, the required clearances and an intact finish are important parts of the installation. Choose primed boards with field painting included or a factory-finished ExpertFinish product, and keep finish coverage separate from substrate coverage.

James Hardie offers rigid fiber cement lap, shingle and panel profiles. The selected HardieZone product, fastening, clearances and opening details belong in the plan. Compare factory-finished ColorPlus with primed products that require painting; both still need periodic inspection and appropriate cleaning.

Real hail damage is random. Hits land scattered across a slope in different sizes, and the same storm marks the metal, siding and screens around the roof. A neat row of marks, or damage on one spot only, usually points to something else. Look from the ground or a window. Checking the roof surface is our job.

How a bruise shows up A dark, roughly round spot, often with granules pressed in or missing It gives slightly under a fingertip, like a soft spot on fruit. A blister doesn't. Bruises sit at random across the slope, more of them on the side that faced the storm They may not leak right away. The weakened spot can shed granules and crack later, which is why bruises are photographed and counted, not ignored.

What granule loss does and doesn't prove Bare black spots on the shingle face, and heavy granules at downspout outlets after a storm Every roof sheds some granules with age, and new roofs shed loose ones in the first months. Granules in the gutter alone don't prove hail damage. What matters is exposed asphalt at impact points, matched to the storm date

Why fractures matter most A fracture is a break through the shingle. It can let water reach the underlayment. Fractures are hard to see from the ground and often show only when the shingle is lifted or flexed by hand The impact test behind Class 4 ratings fails a shingle when a crack shows on the back after two hits in the same spot, which is why fractures are treated as functional damage

What dents tell us Dents show that hail hit and roughly how big it was, and which direction it came from A dented vent can be cosmetic, but a split or crushed one can leak Metal damage is recorded on its own line. A dented vent doesn't by itself mean the shingles failed.

Cosmetic or functional Dents along the front lip and the top of downspout elbows A gutter that still holds its slope and drains is often cosmetic. Split seams, crushed sections or pulled hangers aren't. Gutter work is quoted separately and handled through ourgutter services

Check the side that faced the storm Cracked or holed vinyl siding, chipped paint on wood or fiber cement, dented aluminum trim Torn or dented window screens and dented metal window wraps Spatter marks on decks, fences and outdoor equipment help date the storm Siding repairs go through oursiding services ; windows throughwindows

Look-alikes we rule out Blisters: raised or popped bubbles from trapped moisture or heat. No bruise underneath. Normal wear: even granule thinning across a whole slope, often worst on the south and west faces Foot traffic or tools: scuffs near walkways, ladders and the ridge Old repairs or manufacturing marks: patterns that repeat across the roof. Hail doesn't make patterns.

Size isn't everything. Shingle type, age, wind and the angle of impact all change what a storm does. Still, size is the first thing an adjuster and a roofer ask about, so it helps to know the reference points.
Size comparisons Quarter: 1 inch, the severe threshold Half dollar: roughly 1¼ inches Size means the diameter of the hailstone.

What one state regulator advises homeowners The Nebraska Department of Insurance says hail generally needs to be about 1¼ inches across before it damages a roof. Lightweight composite shingles can show damage from 1-inch hail, and only deteriorated shingles are usually damaged by hail under 1 inch. An older, brittle roof can be damaged by hail a newer roof shrugs off, which is why we look at the roof's age and condition alongside the storm.
Why one slope can look worse Slopes, walls and screens facing the storm take more and harder hits. Slopes on the far side can be untouched. We record each slope separately for that reason.

Where storm reports come from NOAA's Storm Events Database records hail where someone reported it, such as a trained spotter, a law-enforcement officer or a member of the public. A report a mile away doesn't prove your roof was hit, and no nearby report doesn't prove it wasn't. Hail falls in narrow, uneven bands. Your own dated photos of hail on the ground, dented cars or spatter marks are often the best record.

If hail means new shingles, it's worth looking at impact-rated lines. A UL 2218 Class 4 rating means samples survived a controlled test with a 2-inch steel ball. It's the highest class in that test. It doesn't make a roof hail-proof, and the rating describes new product in a lab.

Class 1 to Class 4 Each class uses a larger steel ball. Class 4, the highest, uses a 2-inch ball dropped from 20 feet. The steel-ball size isn't a guaranteed safe hailstone size. Real hail varies in shape, density and speed. A shingle passes if no crack is visible on the back after two impacts in the same spot. FM 4473 uses the same class sizes Manufacturers reach Class 4 with a reinforcing scrim on the back or with polymer-modified (rubberized) asphalt that flexes on impact

What the test doesn't cover Standard impact tests don't account for weathering, temperature or aging. Ridge caps and accessories may not carry the same rating as the field shingle. Ratings apply to labeled packages, so the bundle on your roof should match the line on the proposal.

How to use them IBHS grades shingles Excellent, Good, Marginal or Poor on dents, tears and granule loss. Its most recent ratings were released on November 19, 2025. Ask us to check where a line you're considering stands on the current list.

What to ask your insurer Whether your policy offers a credit for a Class 4 roof, and what proof it needs (product name and installation paperwork) Whether the credit changes your deductible or how cosmetic damage is covered We give you the product documentation. We can't promise a discount./products/roofing/shingles/gaf/timberline-uhdz/

Manufacturer-stated classification speeds under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual roof performance depends on roof design, exposure and installation; this is not a guaranteed storm speed or wind warranty.
Applies to appropriately labeled packages. Impact testing does not guarantee protection from hail damage; confirm current product labeling.
A laboratory classification is different from a wind warranty or a guaranteed storm speed.
Applies to the labeled product; impact testing does not promise a hail-proof roof.
Manufacturer laboratory classifications; not guaranteed storm speeds.
Product labeling and listed test standard govern the classification. Hail damage is not promised to be covered.

A hail claim is between you and your insurer. We inspect the roof, record what we find and explain the repair estimate so you have clear construction facts to share. Your insurer reviews the claim under your policy and decides coverage and payment.

Roles in a hail claim You report the claim to your insurer, share the records you choose and authorize the work Your insurer inspects through its own adjuster, reviews the claim under the policy and decides coverage and payment Roof King inspects, documents and explains the construction findings and the estimate. If you want us to speak with your insurer, that's agreed with you in writing first.

Why your roofer shouldn't negotiate your settlement Ohio law defines a public insurance adjuster as anyone who, for compensation, acts for or helps an insured negotiate or settle a property claim, or advertises that service. No one may act as one without a certificate of authority from the state's superintendent of insurance. Roof King is a roofing contractor. We don't negotiate settlements or act as your adjuster. If you want someone to represent you, ask the Ohio Department of Insurance about licensed public adjusters. Be cautious of anyone who offers to "handle everything" with your insurer in exchange for signing a contract.

Check your policy Look for the reporting period and any limits on cosmetic damage to roofs or metal. If you're unsure, ask your agent or insurer before the deadline passes. A dated inspection record helps either way.

What each warranty covers GAF's warranties don't cover hail damage as a manufacturing defect, and System Plus doesn't replace storm-damage insurance. Under Roof King's workmanship warranty, storm damage is reviewed under its own applicable terms.

Hail doesn't automatically mean a new roof. The decision comes from how many slopes are damaged, how badly, the roof's age and whether new shingles can be blended in. When the findings point to replacement, we show why. The full replacement guide is onroof replacement .

Signs a repair is enough A handful of bruised or fractured shingles on one or two slopes Dented vents or flashing that can be swapped without disturbing much roofing Surrounding shingles that are still flexible and hold their granules A shingle line that's still made in a close color Seeroof repair .

Signs a repair stops making sense Bruises or fractures on most slopes Widespread granule loss at impact points A brittle, older roof that cracks when shingles are lifted for a repair A discontinued line that can't be matched on a visible slope

What to expect Weathering changes color, and lines get discontinued. We show you the closest available match before work starts, and we're honest when a patch would stand out. Whether insurance pays for matching is a policy question for your insurer.

Two numbers decide what a covered roof claim pays you: the deductible, and whether the roof is valued at replacement cost or actual cash value. Your declarations page shows both.

Ohio's claims rule: the insurer determines actual cash value from the replacement cost at the time of loss, including sales tax, less depreciation, and must give you documentation of the depreciation on request. NAIC's illustration: $15,000 of roof damage with $10,000 of depreciation and a $1,000 deductible pays $4,000 under ACV, against $14,000 under replacement cost. figures, not a Roof King price.

expectedBlocks: Wind can break the seal strips that hold shingle courses down, crease the shingles it lifts, peel ridge caps and roof edges, loosen flashing and bring limbs down onto the roof. Roof King & Restoration provides wind damage roof repair for Columbus homes. We inspect the affected slope, not only the visible gap, photograph what we find and give you a written estimate that names each repair.
Water coming in now? Call (614) 490-0123, describe the active problem and ask about current availability.
Choose what you’re dealing with. Each tab covers what wind does to that part of the roof, what we check and what a proper repair involves.

Severe straight-line wind happens here. On August 11, 2026, the National Weather Service measured an 82 mph gust at John Glenn Columbus International Airport and 70 mph at the Ohio State University Airport, and it attributed widespread Franklin County damage to straight-line winds of 60–80 mph . After a storm like that, the order matters: stay safe, limit water getting in, record the damage, then have the roof inspected.
NWS Franklin County Storm Survey — August 11, 2026

Before anything else Contact emergency services for downed power lines, a structural collapse or fire. If you smell gas, leave the house and contact your gas utility from outside. Stay out of rooms or buildings with visible structural damage until a professional has checked them. Look and photograph from the ground or from inside. Don't climb up or pull at loose shingles, flashing or limbs.

What temporary protection does and doesn't do Inside: move belongings, catch drips and start drying wet materials. The City of Columbus advises starting within 24 to 48 hours to limit mold. On the roof: a temporary cover over an opening is installed where it's appropriate and available. Call (614) 490-0123 and describe the problem so availability can be discussed. Keep receipts for emergency supplies, temporary repairs and professional services. Temporary protection doesn't seal broken shingle bonds or reattach flashing. The estimate should say what it covers and what permanent work remains.

What to record Photos and video of every damaged area inside and out, with the date and time Shingles, ridge pieces, flashing or gutter sections in the yard. Photograph them where they landed and keep them. Ceiling stains, drips and attic wetness Don't throw away damaged items until your insurance carrier says it's acceptable. Ourstorm documentation page explains how inspection photos, the estimate and completed-work records fit together.

Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.

Why the bond matters IBHS notes that wind can lift unsealed shingles and let water seep underneath. New shingles can take one to two months or more to seal in poor conditions. We check courses by hand on the windward slopes, where wind usually breaks the most bonds. A shingle that lifts freely along a whole course points to a wider bond failure, not a single loose piece.

Why a crease counts as damage A crease is a break in the shingle's mat. It won't lie flat again or reseal reliably. Creases usually run in a line across several shingles on the same course. Creased shingles are replaced. Gluing them down leaves the fold in place.

What sits under the gap Exposed nails and nail holes let water track down into the underlayment and deck. We check whether the shingles around the gap were nailed correctly, because nail position affects how a shingle holds in wind. Underlayment and decking under the opening are checked before new shingles go on.

How we read them A heavy pile of granules at the downspouts after a storm is worth mentioning when you call. Scuffs alone may be cosmetic. Scuffs with lifted or creased shingles usually aren't. Hail leaves a different pattern. Seehail damage roof repair if the storm brought both.
Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.

What fails and how it's fixed Caps crack or blow off, exposing the ridge vent or the shingle tops underneath. Hip and ridge caps are made to bend over the seam and are fastened on each side above the sealant strip. A lost run of caps is replaced with a compatible cap product, and the ridge vent is checked for wind damage.

Why the edge needs attention IBHS says the starter strip helps prevent water intrusion and protects against wind uplift at the roof edges. We check the starter course, the drip edge and the first shingle course for lifting. An edge that was never properly started tends to fail again. The estimate should say how the new edge will be built.

What we check Step flashing along walls and dormers, chimney flashing and counterflashing, skylight and vent flanges Bent, lifted or face-caulked pieces are reset or replaced, not coated over The repair names the failed part rather than treating everything as a shingle replacement

Gutters belong in the same inspection Gutters pulled from the fascia can let water behind them onto the fascia board and the roof edge. We note gutter and fascia damage separately on the estimate, not folded into the roof patch. Gutter repair and replacement are covered on ourgutter services page .

A tree or a large limb on the roof is a structural problem first and a roofing problem second. The roof can only be repaired properly once the tree is off and the framing and decking below have been checked.

Safety first If lines are down or the structure is damaged, contact emergency services and stay clear. Photograph the tree on the roof from the ground and the damage from inside before anything is moved. A tree blocking the street can be reported to the City of Columbus. Damage entirely on private property is the owner's and their insurer's responsibility.

What the inspection covers Broken or cracked decking and any damaged rafters or trusses under the impact area Shingles, ridge, flashing and gutters along the path the tree took Siding, fascia and soffit damage where the tree hit the wall line Damaged wood is noted for repair before new roofing goes on

Shingle packages list wind classifications from two different ASTM tests, plus a separate manufacturer wind warranty. They answer three different questions, and none of them means a roof can't be damaged by wind.

What the class means IBHS describes D3161 as measuring a shingle's ability to withstand fan-induced wind speeds. Class F is the highest D3161 class. GAF lists it as 110 mph. The speed describes air flowing over the shingles in the lab, not the wind load on your house.

What the class means IBHS: D7158 assigns a class based on a two-part uplift test, and the classes tie to ASCE 7 wind zones. Class H is the highest D7158 class. GAF lists it as 150 mph. Both tests evaluate new product. IBHS notes they don't account for weathering or aging. An older roof doesn't keep its rating.

What usually decides coverage The stated mph applies to a particular product, installed a particular way. Higher wind coverage often requires the manufacturer's starter, ridge and other accessories, extra nails or a special application. The product cards below show each line's conditions. Shingles generally need to have sealed. Damage from falling trees or debris is a different matter from blow-off. Your proposal names the product, and the manufacturer's warranty document sets the terms.

Manufacturer-stated classification speeds under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual roof performance depends on roof design, exposure and installation; this is not a guaranteed storm speed or wind warranty.
Applies to appropriately labeled packages. Impact testing does not guarantee protection from hail damage; confirm current product labeling.
A laboratory classification is different from a wind warranty or a guaranteed storm speed.
Applies to the labeled product; impact testing does not promise a hail-proof roof.
Manufacturer laboratory classifications; not guaranteed storm speeds.
Product labeling and listed test standard govern the classification. Hail damage is not promised to be covered.

Wind is a common reason homeowners file a property claim. Your insurer decides whether the damage is covered and what it pays. Roof King's job is the roof: we inspect it, document what wind did, explain our findings and give you a written estimate for the work.

What the City of Columbus advises Contact your insurance carrier right away if you believe the property was damaged. Policies have deadlines for reporting claims. For help understanding a policy or disputing a decision, the Ohio Department of Insurance is at insurance.ohio.gov or insurance.ohio.gov. A roofing estimate doesn't decide whether a claim is approved or what it pays.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

Our part Inspection photos tied to locations on the roof, and written findings A written estimate that names the materials, the repairs and any adjoining work Completed-work records once the job is done You may share our construction findings and estimate with your insurer. Coverage and payment discussions remain between you and your insurer.

What Ohio law says Ohio defines a public insurance adjuster as anyone who, for compensation, acts on behalf of an insured in settling a property loss claim. That work requires a certificate of authority from the state. We stick to the roof. If you want someone to represent you on the claim, that's a licensed public adjuster or an attorney.
Ohio Public Adjuster Licensing Requirements

The Ohio matching rule When a replacement-cost policy pays to replace an item and the replacement doesn't match in quality, color or size, Ohio's claims rule requires the insurer to replace as much of the item as needed for a reasonably comparable appearance. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's decision under your policy. We document the product on your roof and what's currently available.

The City's checklist Confirm the contractor is registered with the Ohio Secretary of State. Get more than one estimate and a written contract before work starts. Don't pay in full upfront. Report suspected contractor fraud to the Ohio Attorney General through the agency's official website. Residential roofing in Columbus falls under the City's Home Improvement limited contractor license, which you can look up on the Citizen Access Portal.
Most wind damage is repairable. Wind alone doesn't make a roof a replacement case, and you should expect a clear reason before anyone recommends one.

Signs a repair will hold Missing or creased shingles on a few courses, a run of ridge caps or one flashing detail Shingles next to the damage still lie flat, seal and bend without cracking A compatible product is available, and you've seen how the color will compare

Signs a repair won't last Seal strips broken across whole slopes, not just a few courses Old shingles crack when lifted to weave in new ones Repeated blow-offs, or decking damage across a large area Ourroof replacement page covers materials, decking and what a full estimate includes.
What to ask Ask whether your project needs a permit and who will pull it. Properties in special zoning or historic districts may need extra approvals. Suburbs outside city limits set their own rules.

As our offers pages describe them System Plus: qualifying GAF shingles, at least three qualifying accessories and an eligible GAF-certified contractor. It extends initial non-prorated coverage for eligible products. Silver Pledge: four qualifying accessories and a Certified Plus or Master Elite contractor. It adds coverage for installation errors, for a period that depends on the shingle. Golden Pledge: five qualifying accessories, Master Elite contractors only, with installation-error coverage. These apply to new qualifying GAF roof systems, not to spot repairs. SeeGAF System Plus for the full terms.

The inspection follows the shingle courses beyond the obvious gap. Lifted or unsealed tabs, creases and backed-out fasteners help identify how far the affected area extends. Retained shingles must be suitable for a compatible repair.

Creases and lifted tabs are recorded with their location so the photographs match the estimate’s repair items. You receive construction findings whether paying directly or submitting documents to your insurer.

The assessment considers fastening, starter courses, drip edge, ridge caps and flashing, plus attic daylight or wet decking where accessible. An isolated patch should not leave an identified failed connection or damaged underlying layer unresolved.

Affected areas, photographs and roof locations.Missing, creased and unsealed courses included in the repair.Ridge caps, starter, drip edge and flashing being reset or replaced.Underlayment and decking repairs revealed by the damage.Temporary protection and the permanent work that remains.Separate gutter, fascia, siding and interior work.

Identify the shingle line, profile, finish and related flashings. Discuss aging, discontinued products and how close a replacement can match the retained roof. Include the adjoining repairs needed to restore the affected connection.

There's no single number. Shingle age, how well the courses sealed, nailing, roof shape and exposure all matter. Wind ratings are measured on new shingles in a lab, and IBHS notes the tests don't account for weathering or aging. Older roofs, edges and ridges usually fail first. After any storm that sends shingles into the yard, have the roof checked.

Most wind damage is repairable. A repair makes sense when the damage is confined to identifiable areas and the surrounding shingles still seal and bend without cracking. Replacement belongs in the conversation when seal strips have failed across whole slopes or the old shingles are too brittle to work. You'll get the reason in writing either way. Seeroof repair for repairs beyond storm damage.

Often closely, but rarely perfectly. Weathering, color batches and discontinued lines all affect the match. We identify your shingle, show you the closest current product and tell you how it will look before work starts. For insured losses on a replacement-cost policy, Ohio's claims rule requires the insurer to replace enough for a reasonably comparable appearance. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's call.

That depends on your policy and is decided by your insurer, not by Roof King. Contact your carrier promptly, because policies have reporting deadlines. No. In Ohio, acting for a homeowner in settling a property claim for compensation is public insurance adjusting, which requires a state certificate of authority. We explain our construction findings and the proposed work. You may share our written construction findings with your insurer; coverage and payment remain between you and the insurer.

Get everyone clear. Contact emergency services if power lines are down or the structure looks unsafe, and stay out of damaged rooms. Photograph the tree and the damage from the ground and from inside before anything is moved, and contact your insurer. Once the tree is off, the roof inspection should check the decking and framing under the impact, not just the shingles.

Inside City of Columbus limits, replacing a roof requires a building permit, with no plan review. Properties in special zoning or historic districts may need extra approvals. Ask whether your repair needs a permit and who will pull it. Suburbs outside the city set their own rules.

ASTM D3161 (up to Class F) and ASTM D7158 (up to Class H) are two different lab tests of new shingles. A limited wind warranty is the manufacturer's coverage, and higher speeds often depend on qualifying accessories and installation. For example, GAF's WindProven coverage requires a qualifying system. Will replacement windows eliminate drafts?

Properly selected and installed windows can address drafts caused by deteriorated units or poor connections, but drafts may also come from other parts of the home. The source should be identified before making promises.
Will new windows stop condensation?
Not always. Condensation can involve indoor humidity, temperature, ventilation or a failed insulated glass unit. The location and cause matter.
Can I replace only a few windows?
Yes, replacing windows in stages may be practical. Plan for matching profiles, finishes and product availability if you expect to complete other openings later.
What is the difference between insert and full-frame replacement?
An insert may retain suitable portions of an existing frame. Fuller removal exposes more of the opening and may be needed where the frame or surrounding construction is damaged.

We discuss energy-efficient replacement windows using the proposed product line, glass package and NFRC ratings. Those details belong in your written proposal.

Yes, the window-to-wall connections and finishing details should be planned together when siding work is also proposed.

Timing depends on the number and type of windows, product availability, opening condition and finishing work.

cards.title: Signs of Wind Damage on a Residential Roof

children.text: Wind commonly affects roof edges, ridges and areas around chimneys or other projections. Some damage is visible from the yard; other conditions require a trained inspection.
Missing, displaced or creased shingles.
Lifted shingles or broken sealant bonds that may be difficult to see from the ground.
Loose ridge caps, drip edge or flashing around chimneys, skylights and vents.
Shingle pieces, nails or roofing debris found in the yard.
Gutters or siding pulled loose by wind or falling limbs.
A shingle that has lifted and settled back into place may still have a compromised seal. That is one reason a roof can leak during the next storm even when no shingles appear to be missing.

cards.title: What Hail Damage Looks Like

children.text: Hail can affect shingles, roof vents, soft-metal flashing and gutters. Dents in metal are worth documenting, but they do not by themselves prove that every nearby shingle is damaged. Hail size, roof age, material and the angle of impact all matter.

On asphalt shingles, an inspector looks for impact-related surface changes and distinguishes them from normal wear, blistering, foot traffic or older damage. A proper assessment explains the location and significance of the findings rather than relying on a single close-up photo.
If you see dented gutters, granules near downspouts or marks on roof accessories after a hailstorm, report them when requesting the inspection. Avoid rubbing, lifting or testing shingles yourself.
